items.text:
We built NariQ: 3-bit-or-lower quantizations of Qwen3.8-27B that retain near-BF16 quality across agentic tasks, math, multilingual reasoning, and image understanding.

To our knowledge, this is the first 3-bit-or-lower quantization that retains BF16 lvl performance on long-horizon agentic tasks.

Benchmarks (BF16 / 3-bit / 2.5-bit / 2-bit):

- DeepSWE: 39.8 / 41.0 / 41.9 / 28.6

- Terminal-Bench 2.1: 62.6 / 63.8 / 60.2 / 52.4

- AIME 25+26: 97.7 / 98.3 / 96.5 / 86.0

- MSGM: 94.0 / 93.1 / 91.8 / 90.6

- RealWorldQA: 82.4 / 82.4 / 81.3 / 80.9

Decode speed is comparable to other quants on an RTX PRO 6000. Context-length results below

(3-bit / 2.5-bit / 2-bit / Unsloth UD-IQ3_XXS):

- 4K: 88.9 / 99.2 / 111.7 / 94.7

- 16K: 84.5 / 93.8 / 105.1 / 89.8

- 64K: 70.7 / 77.5 / 85.0 / 74.8

Running these currently require our llama.cpp fork: (https://github.com/nari-labs/nari-llama.cpp)

Feedback and questions welcome. We'd love to hear how these perform on your workloads.

items.text:
I was about to keep track of my clients and prospecting in Google Sheets for my solopreneur business, when I remembered that's exactly what I advise my clients not to do.

Created Hermit CRM, an open source CRM for 1 person. Hermit helps to keep track of deals and prospecting. The platform is built for AI by storing the data in Markdown files in git, stored locally and can be accessed with a web app, CLI or MCP. No telemetry on the app. Building in public, even the website stats are public as well.

It’s macOS first. Linux is less tested, and Windows isn’t supported.

Features I'm proud of: - import somebody from LinkedIn into to the CRM with 1 click - adding a LinkedIn convo to the CRM with 1 click. Both work without LinkedIn or CRM subs.

Don't like what you see? Fork the Hermit with your AI.

Would love to learn how you're using Hermit and where it doesn't fit your workflows.
items.title: Show HN: Hermit CRM – Free open-source CRM for solopreneurs

items.text: just joined this new team about 1 year into their development. Demoed the work to the team about two weeks ago (half way in). Work is practically complete & runs well no issues. I create PR & assign the two PR reviewers (one my rank another a rank above me). one colleague (the one at my level) leaves some constructive comments no functional changes. The other colleague (one rank above me) says something equivalent to "does not meet our standards" "do not do x pattern since we have used y (which has a huge limitation)" to use Y pattern I would basically need to change most of the logic and it would be about 70% waste. I demoed my code with this pattern two weeks ago and there were no issues/comments from the team. The code is concise and easy to read. I had a call with the colleague and explained the code and why I used it, and showed him some other parts of the codebase where this pattern should be used, his only defense was that "it does not meet our standards because it uses X rather than y pattern, since we used y pattern in the past, we should only use y pattern" while x pattern is very similar only removing the limitation that was causing the code to be difficult to maintain etc. This "standard requirement" is written nowhere as a hard requirement and the codebase is barely one year old, with only one of the codebase founders still on the team.... I'm going to have a chat with the manager tomorrow morning.

items.text:
Hi everyone, we love maps and doing some fun side quests exploring this domain.

We were always surprised by the fact that products like ChatGpt recommends you places to go which have been shut down for years.

Last March we built a benchmark measuring how often LLMs make mistakes when answering places-based queries (e.g. Recommend me a restaurant in Marina for a dinner). Even with the web grounding (which is a very expensive tool relative to the token price), the results were not good - 1 out 10 places in the best model were made up or shut-down.

When personal assistants started to come up, we were curious to check how well they do with those queries. It turns out that much better, but they also take longer time to answer. We make it slightly more challenging, we made a benchmark a bit more sophisticated and measured it.

The best one turned out to be Dots from OpenAI, and it is also one of the fastest. The worst one was Grok Bot from XAI. We also measured Ask Maps from Google, but it was out of competition, because it is not technically a personal assistant. The more detailed results are available in the repository
